choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from a cost comparison and offered in support of a further conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a consideration the argument concedes before rejecting it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background information that plays no role in the reasoning.

items.explanation: Run the two-way test. What supports 'the restoration pays for itself'? The nine-versus-fourteen million comparison. What does it support? The recommendation to fund it now. Supported and supporting: an intermediate conclusion — C. A names the wrong tier; the main conclusion is the final sentence's recommendation. B is wrong because the cost comparison is exactly its support. D describes a concession, but nothing here is granted and then rejected. E is contradicted by the 'so' that introduces it.

items.stem:
A four-year study of a court's mandatory mediation program found that mediated cases settled at nearly the same rate as unmediated ones, but that mediated cases which settled did so an average of five months earlier. Mediated cases that did not settle went to trial no later than comparable unmediated cases.

The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory mediation causes cases to settle that would not otherwise have settled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mediation program should be adopted by every court in the jurisdiction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The program's principal effect is on the timing of settlements rather than on how many cases settle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cases that go to trial after mediation are resolved more quickly than those that go to trial without it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Litigants who participate in mediation are more satisfied with the outcome than those who do not.

items.explanation: Settlement rates were 'nearly the same' while settled cases resolved five months earlier, and non-settling cases were not delayed. The claim the findings best support is that the program moves timing, not volume — C, and note how modestly it is worded. A is contradicted by the equal settlement rates. B is a recommendation the data alone cannot license, and 'every court' overreaches. D reverses the third finding, which says trial timing was *no later*, not earlier. E introduces satisfaction, which the study never measured.

items.stem:
Every associate who bills more than two thousand hours receives the annual bonus. No associate in the pro bono rotation receives the annual bonus. At least one associate in the pro bono rotation was promoted this year.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some associates who bill more than two thousand hours were not promoted this year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No associate in the pro bono rotation bills more than two thousand hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some associates who received the annual bonus were not promoted this year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every associate who was promoted this year bills more than two thousand hours.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every associate outside the pro bono rotation received the annual bonus.

items.explanation: Chain the first two statements: billing over two thousand hours guarantees the bonus, and rotation members never get the bonus, so by contrapositive no rotation member bills over two thousand hours. The third statement puts at least one rotation member among this year's promotions. D says every promoted associate bills over two thousand — but that promoted rotation member does not, so D collides with the derived inference and cannot be true. B is the trap: it states the derived inference itself, so far from being impossible it MUST be true. A, C, and E are each consistent — nothing links billing or the bonus to promotion in either direction, and nothing bars the firm from paying the bonus to everyone outside the rotation.

items.stem:
Two years ago the hospital introduced a checklist that surgical teams must complete before every operation. Since then, the rate of post-operative infection has fallen by a third. The checklist is therefore responsible for the decline.

Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How long it takes a surgical team to complete the checklist

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the hospital adopted any other infection-control measure during the same two years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether other hospitals in the region have adopted similar checklists

choices.label: D
choices.text: What the post-operative infection rate was three years before the checklist was introduced

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether surgical teams find the checklist burdensome

items.explanation: Apply the variance test. If the hospital adopted no other measure, the checklist's claim to credit is much stronger; if it also, say, changed its sterilization protocol, an alternative cause is live and the argument weakens. B swings the argument both ways. A and E bear on cost and morale, not on whether the checklist caused the decline. C tells us about other hospitals' choices, which leaves this hospital's causal story untouched. D is tempting — a trend already falling would weaken — but a single earlier figure establishes no trend, so either answer leaves the argument roughly where it was.

items.stem:
Every witness who testified at the hearing was placed under oath. Okonkwo did not testify at the hearing. It does not follow that Okonkwo was not placed under oath, because ___

Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: some witnesses who testify are not credible

choices.label: B
choices.text: people other than testifying witnesses are sometimes placed under oath

choices.label: C
choices.text: Okonkwo was present at the hearing

choices.label: D
choices.text: the hearing officer has discretion over who testifies

choices.label: E
choices.text: not every person placed under oath tells the truth

items.explanation: The connector is 'because', so the blank wants the premise that licenses the stated conclusion. The argument says the inference fails — and it fails precisely because 'all testifying witnesses were sworn' leaves open that non-witnesses were sworn too. B supplies exactly that. A and E are about credibility and truthfulness, which the argument never touches. C is topical but does nothing: being present neither implies nor excludes being sworn. D explains who testifies, not who is sworn.

items.stem:
Last year the public defender's office resolved a smaller percentage of its cases by plea than it did a decade ago. Clearly, then, fewer of the office's clients are pleading guilty than a decade ago.

The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the ground that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes for granted that a decline in a proportion establishes a decline in an absolute number

choices.label: B
choices.text: confuses a claim about the public defender's office with a claim about defence counsel generally

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes without warrant that pleading guilty is undesirable

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on a sample of cases too small to support a general conclusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a correlation between two trends as though it established a causal link

items.explanation: The premise is a share ('a smaller percentage'); the conclusion is a count ('fewer clients'). Both can be true only if the caseload did not grow — and if it grew enough, a smaller share is a larger number. A names the switch. B alleges a scope shift the argument does not make; it stays with one office throughout. C imports an evaluative assumption the argument never needs. D complains about sample size, but the argument reports the office's own caseload rather than sampling it. E describes a causal flaw in an argument that draws no causal conclusion.

items.stem:
The bar association mailed a survey to all of its members asking whether the continuing-education requirement should be increased. Of the members who returned the survey, sixty-two percent said it should. The association concluded that most of its members favour an increase.

The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: fails to consider that members might change their views over time

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats members who returned the survey as representative of members generally, though members with strong views about the requirement are likelier to have responded

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a policy from evidence about opinions

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from a sample that is too small to be reliable

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that what most members favour is what the association should do

items.explanation: The sample selected itself: only members who chose to return the survey are counted, and an opinion question about a burdensome requirement is exactly the kind that motivates the strongly-opinionated to respond. B names the mismatch between how the sample was assembled and the population concluded about. A raises a timing worry the argument does not depend on. C misdescribes the conclusion, which is about member opinion, not about policy. D reaches for sample size — the tempting wrong answer here, since nothing tells us the response count was small, and size was never the defect. E attacks a normative step the argument never takes.

items.stem:
Critics who dismiss the novel as sentimental have simply failed to read it with the attention it deserves. We know this because anyone who reads the novel attentively comes to recognize that its emotional directness is a deliberate technique rather than a lapse in craft — and no one who recognizes that would call the book sentimental.

The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the ground that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a claim to be false merely because those who assert it are unqualified

choices.label: B
choices.text: presupposes what it purports to establish, by defining attentive reading as reading that reaches the author's own verdict

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about all critics from evidence about some of them

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a sufficient condition for attentive reading with a necessary one

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on an appeal to the authority of readers who share the author's view

items.explanation: The conclusion is that dismissive critics read inattentively. The support is that attentive readers all reach the opposite verdict — which is true only because the argument has built the verdict into what 'attentive' means. Accepting the premise requires already accepting the conclusion: B. A describes an ad hominem, and the argument attacks the reading rather than the reader's standing. C alleges hasty generalization, but the claim covers exactly the critics the premise is about. D names a conditional confusion the argument does not commit — its conditional runs one direction throughout. E is close in flavour and wrong in mechanism: no authority is invoked; the circle is definitional.

items.stem:
Ferreira: Requiring judicial nominees to answer questions about specific pending controversies would compromise their impartiality. A nominee who has publicly committed to a view cannot later decide the matter with an open mind.

Wong: Nominees already have views; the hearing only reveals them. What compromises impartiality is deciding a case one has prejudged, and that risk exists whether or not the prejudgment was ever spoken aloud.

Ferreira and Wong disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: judicial nominees typically hold views about pending controversies

choices.label: B
choices.text: publicly stating a view about a controversy makes a nominee less able to decide it impartially than holding that view privately does

choices.label: C
choices.text: impartiality is a desirable quality in a judge

choices.label: D
choices.text: confirmation hearings serve any useful purpose

choices.label: E
choices.text: a judge who has prejudged a case should recuse from it

items.explanation: Ferreira's argument turns on the *public commitment* doing the damage; Wong's reply is that the damage is done by the prejudgment itself, so speaking it aloud adds nothing. That comparative claim is the disagreement — B. A is Wong's premise and Ferreira does not deny it; indeed Ferreira's worry presupposes nominees can form views. C is common ground. D is never addressed by Ferreira. E is a remedy neither speaker discusses, which is what makes it a clean failure of the two-part test.

items.stem:
An insurer analyzed two of its regional call centres. At the Northern centre, claims handlers who completed the optional fraud-detection training referred four percent of claims for investigation; handlers who did not complete it referred two percent. At the Southern centre the same gap appeared. The insurer concluded that the training makes handlers better at detecting fraud, and it made the training mandatory company-wide.

Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the insurer's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What proportion of referred claims were ultimately confirmed to be fraudulent, among handlers who had completed the training and among those who had not

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the two regional centres handle claims of comparable value

choices.label: C
choices.text: How many handlers at each centre completed the optional training

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether handlers who completed the training had been employed longer than those who had not

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether the company-wide mandatory training uses the same curriculum as the optional version

items.explanation: The conclusion is about *detection* — finding fraud — but every figure in the stimulus is a referral rate, which measures suspicion, not accuracy. A goes straight to that gap: if trained handlers' referrals are confirmed as fraud at the same or a higher rate, the training is detecting better; if their extra referrals are overwhelmingly unfounded, the training merely made them refer more. Both answers move the argument decisively. D is the strong distractor — it supplies an alternative cause, self-selection by tenure — but it is second best, because even a perfect answer leaves the referral-versus-detection gap untouched: longer-tenured handlers referring more still tells us nothing about whether those referrals were right. B and C bear on comparability and sample size without touching the inference from referrals to detection. E concerns the remedy the insurer adopted rather than the conclusion it drew.

items.stem:
Council member: The protected bike lane on Third Street will slow the buses that share the corridor, and riders on those routes will feel it. But the delay is smaller than the one drivers already impose on the buses by double-parking, and the lane will pull cyclists out of the bus lane, where they slow buses most. The lane should be built this year.

The claim that the bike lane will slow the buses that share the corridor plays which one of the following roles in the council member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion the council member argues for.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is evidence offered in direct support of the recommendation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a claim the council member argues is false.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a cost the council member grants and then argues is outweighed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an assumption required for the recommendation to follow.

items.explanation: The sentence is introduced as a real drawback and is immediately met with 'But' — the mark of a concession the arguer accepts and then answers. D says exactly that. A misreads the tier: the conclusion is the last sentence's recommendation. B has the support running the wrong way; a cost of building the lane cannot be evidence for building it. C is wrong because the council member never disputes that buses will be slowed, only that the delay is decisive. E confuses a conceded objection with a required premise; the argument would be stronger, not broken, if the delay did not exist.

items.stem:
In one state's small-claims court, litigants may appear with or without a lawyer. Cases in which neither side has a lawyer are resolved, on average, in half the time of cases in which at least one side does. When one side has a lawyer and the other does not, the represented side prevails substantially more often than the unrepresented side. When both sides have lawyers, neither side prevails more often than the other.

The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A litigant in this court who hires a lawyer is more likely to prevail than one who does not, whatever the opposing side does.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether hiring a lawyer improves a litigant's chances in this court depends on whether the opposing side also has one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cases resolved quickly in this court are more likely to be decided correctly than cases resolved slowly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most litigants who appear in this court appear without a lawyer.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lawyers lengthen proceedings in this court by raising issues the court would not otherwise have to resolve.

items.explanation: Put the two outcome facts side by side: a lawyer against an unrepresented opponent wins substantially more often, and a lawyer against another lawyer wins no more often. The advantage therefore turns on what the other side does, which is B. A overstates it into a claim the third fact directly contradicts. C rates accuracy, which the stimulus never measures. D is about how common representation is; the stimulus gives averages, not proportions of litigants. E converts a reported association between representation and duration into a causal mechanism the facts do not establish.

items.stem:
Every grant application the ethics panel reviews is either funded or returned for revision. No application returned for revision is reviewed again in the same funding cycle. An application submitted after March 1 is reviewed by the panel only if a director sponsors it. Every sponsored application is funded.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An application submitted before March 1 was returned for revision.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An application was funded although no director sponsored it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A director sponsored an application that was submitted before March 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An application submitted after March 1 was reviewed by the panel and returned for revision.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An application returned for revision in one funding cycle was reviewed in a later cycle.

items.explanation: Chain the last two conditions. Reviewed and submitted after March 1 means sponsored; sponsored means funded; and funded rules out returned for revision, since the first sentence makes the two outcomes exclusive. D asserts all of that at once, so D cannot be true. A and C concern applications the March 1 rule never reaches. B is consistent: sponsorship guarantees funding but is nowhere made necessary for it. E is barred only within the same cycle, and E moves to a later one.

items.stem:
Digitizing a court's paper files reduces the time clerks spend retrieving records, but it does not by itself reduce the court's backlog. The backlog forms at the hearing stage, where the number of judges available to hear matters, and not the speed with which files reach them, sets the pace at which cases clear. So a court that digitizes its files without adding judges should expect ______

Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: its backlog to fall roughly in proportion to the time its clerks save.

choices.label: B
choices.text: its backlog to grow more quickly than it did before digitization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: its clerks' retrieval work to fall while its backlog stays roughly where it was.

choices.label: D
choices.text: its clerks to spend more time retrieving records than they did before.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the number of judges available to hear matters to fall.

items.explanation: The passage grants one effect and denies another: retrieval time drops, the backlog does not, because judges rather than files are the bottleneck. C is that pair of results and nothing more, so C completes the argument. A asserts the very drop the second sentence rules out. B goes further still, predicting a worsening the passage gives no reason to expect. D contradicts the first sentence. E introduces a change in judicial staffing that the passage neither states nor implies.

items.stem:
The number of appeals filed in this state's intermediate appellate court rose by thirty percent over the last decade. Appellate work must therefore make up a larger share of the state's legal practice than it did ten years ago.

The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the ground that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes without warrant that the additional appeals filed were meritorious

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats an increase in appeals filed as though it were an increase in appeals decided

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a period longer than the one its evidence covers

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that the rise in filings was caused by an increase in errors at trial

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers a change in a proportion from a change in an absolute number, with no information about the total

items.explanation: The evidence is a count of appeals; the conclusion is appellate work's share of all legal practice. If every other kind of legal work grew by thirty percent as well, the share is unchanged, and if the rest grew faster, the share fell. E names that missing denominator. A and D attack quality and cause, neither of which the conclusion is about. B alleges a filed-versus-decided switch, but the conclusion concerns work performed, which filings do measure. C is false on the face of it: evidence and conclusion cover the same decade.

items.stem:
To gauge local opinion on the new zoning ordinance, a newspaper invited readers to submit comments through its website. Of the four hundred comments received, three hundred forty opposed the ordinance. The newspaper reported that most residents of the town oppose it.

The newspaper's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about residents' opinions from evidence about the ordinance's merits

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that a single reader may have submitted more than one comment

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats people who chose to respond as though they represented the population as a whole

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that opposition to a zoning ordinance shows the ordinance to be unwise

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that opinion will shift once the ordinance takes effect

items.explanation: Nobody selected these respondents but themselves, and the residents most moved to write are the residents who object. A self-selected sample cannot support a claim about everyone, which is C. B names a real hygiene problem with web comments, but even one comment per person leaves the sample self-selected, so it is not what breaks the inference. A misdescribes the evidence, which is opinion rather than merit. D and E answer questions the newspaper never asked: whether the ordinance is wise, and what residents will think later.

items.stem:
Attorney: My client's account of the accident is credible. He would never lie under oath, as we know from the fact that he is a credible witness.

The reasoning in the attorney's argument is flawed in that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on the testimony of someone with an interest in the outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition that is necessary for credibility as though it were sufficient

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes about all of the client's statements from a single one

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes the truth of the very claim it is supposed to establish

choices.label: E
choices.text: criticizes those who doubt the client instead of answering their reasons

items.explanation: The conclusion is that the client is credible; the support offered is that he would not lie under oath; the support for that is that he is credible. The chain returns to its starting point, which is D. B describes a conditional confusion, but nothing here is offered as a necessary condition. A is a fair observation about interested witnesses and no part of this argument's structure. C invents a generalization the attorney never makes. E describes an ad hominem, and the attorney attacks no one.

items.stem:
Every witness who testified on Monday was cross-examined. Ruiz testified on Monday.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ruiz testified only on Monday.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every witness who was cross-examined testified on Monday.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some witnesses who testified on Monday were not cross-examined.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ruiz was the only witness cross-examined on Monday.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ruiz was cross-examined.

items.explanation: The first sentence is a conditional — testified Monday, therefore cross-examined — and the second supplies the condition for Ruiz. E follows and nothing more does. B reverses the conditional, which is not an inference the premises license. C contradicts the first sentence outright. A and D add exclusivity claims — only Monday, only Ruiz — that the premises never mention.

items.stem:
The city's recycling program costs more per tonne than sending the same waste to a landfill. But the landfill will reach capacity in six years, and the nearest alternative site is ninety kilometres away. The city should keep funding the recycling program.

Which one of the following is the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city should keep funding the recycling program.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The recycling program costs more per tonne than landfilling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The landfill will reach capacity within six years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nearest alternative landfill site is ninety kilometres away.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recycling will become cheaper than landfilling within six years.

items.explanation: The last sentence is the recommendation everything else is offered to support, which makes A the main conclusion. B is the cost fact the argument concedes, and C and D are the two considerations offered against it. E is a prediction the argument never makes; it claims the landfill will fill up, not that recycling will become the cheaper option.

items.stem:
The clinic's new intake form is shorter than the old one. Clients will therefore complete it more quickly.

The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The old intake form was longer than any other form the clinic uses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clients who complete the form quickly are more likely to return.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The clinic's staff prefer the new intake form to the old one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new form's questions are not harder to answer than the old form's.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No client will need help completing the new form.

items.explanation: Shorter does not mean faster if the remaining questions are harder to answer; the argument needs that possibility ruled out, which is D. Negate it and the conclusion collapses. A compares the old form with other forms, which the argument never does. B adds a benefit of speed the conclusion does not claim. C reports a preference the argument does not rely on. E is far stronger than the argument needs: some clients could need help and the form could still be quicker on average.

items.stem:
After the library began opening on Sundays, weekly visits rose by a fifth. The Sunday hours must be what drew the additional visitors.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The library's Sunday staff are the same people who work on Saturdays.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most libraries in the region are closed on Sundays.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A new bus route serving the library opened in the same week as the Sunday hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Visits on Saturdays fell slightly after the Sunday hours began.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The library's collection has not grown since the Sunday hours began.

items.explanation: The argument treats the Sunday hours as the cause of the rise. C supplies a rival cause that arrived at exactly the same time, which is the standard way a causal claim of this shape is undermined. D is the tempting answer, but a small fall on Saturdays is consistent with a fifth more visits overall and does nothing to explain where the extra visitors came from. A and E report facts that leave the causal question untouched, and B, if anything, helps the argument by making the library unusual in the region.

items.stem:
Critic: A restoration is faithful only if it uses the materials the original artisans used. The chapel's roof was restored with modern tiles, so the restoration is not faithful — and since the trust funds only faithful restorations, it will not fund this one.

Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dish is authentic only if it is cooked in a clay pot. This stew was cooked in a clay pot, so it is authentic, and the guide lists only authentic dishes, so it will list this stew.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A grant is renewable only if the project reports on time. This project reported late, so its grant is not renewable — and since the board renews only renewable grants, it will not renew this one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A translation is accurate only if the translator knows both languages. This translator knows both languages, so the translation may well be accurate, and the press publishes translations that may well be accurate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A building is historic only if it is more than a century old. The annex is ninety years old, so it is not historic, and the registry lists most historic buildings, so it probably will not list the annex.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A claim is admissible only if it is filed within a year. This claim was filed within a year, so it is admissible, and the tribunal hears only admissible claims, so it will hear this one.

items.explanation: The original runs: X only if Y; not Y; so not X; and since only X gets the benefit, this one does not. Two moves, both valid — denying the necessary condition, then applying a second necessary condition to withhold the benefit. B repeats both exactly. A and E instead affirm the necessary condition and conclude the thing holds, which is the invalid converse and so a different pattern, valid or not. C weakens every step to a possibility and reaches no comparable conclusion. D matches the first move but softens the second into 'most' and 'probably', so the conclusion no longer follows as it does in the original.

items.stem:
Principle: A public body may withhold a document only if releasing it would harm an interest the body is charged with protecting, and only if that harm outweighs the public's interest in seeing the document.

Which one of the following judgements most closely conforms to the principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A housing agency withholds a contractor's bid because releasing it would embarrass the contractor, whose reputation the agency has no duty to protect, and because the public interest in the bid is slight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A police service releases an informant's name because the public interest in the case is intense, although disclosure would put the informant at serious risk of harm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A health authority withholds a hospital's inspection report because releasing it would undermine public confidence in the hospital, an interest the authority protects, even though the report bears directly on patient safety.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A water utility withholds a map of its pipe network because releasing it would help vandals disable the supply, which the utility is charged with protecting, and the public can see the same safety data in the utility's annual report.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A school board releases a teacher's disciplinary file because the board's policy is to release all personnel records on request.

items.explanation: The principle permits withholding only when both tests are met: a protected interest is harmed, and that harm outweighs the public's interest in the document. D is the only judgement that satisfies both — the utility's charge is the supply itself, and the public interest is slight because the same safety information is published elsewhere. A fails the first test, since the agency protects no interest in the contractor's reputation. C is the near miss: the interest is protected but a report bearing directly on patient safety is exactly where the public interest is weightiest, so the balance goes the other way. B and E concern releases, and the principle constrains only withholding — neither judgement can conform to it or violate it.

items.stem:
Editor: Every article we publish is fact-checked. An article is published only if two editors have approved it. Kovac approved the article on the bridge collapse, and it was fact-checked. So it will be published.

The reasoning above is most vulnerable to criticism on the ground that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the fact that every published article is fact-checked as though fact-checking guaranteed publication, and treats one editor's approval as though it were two

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes without warrant that Kovac is an editor whose approval counts

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses a claim about the editor's own articles with a claim about every article the publication runs

choices.label: D

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that the second editor's approval might be withdrawn before publication

items.explanation: Two distinct errors, and the credited answer has to name both. Fact-checking is stated as a *consequence* of publication, not a condition for it, so 'it was fact-checked' supports nothing; and two approvals are necessary, so one approval does not supply even the condition that is required. A is the only option that reports both. B raises a question the stimulus settles by calling Kovac an approver in an editor's own argument. D and E invent timing and withdrawal scenarios that leave the two structural errors untouched, and E in particular presupposes a second approval the stimulus never reports. C describes a scope shift the argument does not make.

items.stem:
Two towns drew their drinking water from the same aquifer. After the eastern town installed a filtration plant, reported cases of gastrointestinal illness there fell by a third over five years, while reported cases in the western town, which installed no plant, held steady. Researchers concluded that the plant caused the decline.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The eastern town's plant removes the two organisms most often responsible for waterborne gastrointestinal illness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Physicians in the eastern town report gastrointestinal illness to the regional registry at the same rate as physicians in the western town, and that rate did not change over the five years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The eastern town's population grew slightly over the five years while the western town's was unchanged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residents of both towns drink roughly the same quantity of tap water each day.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The eastern town's council had debated building the filtration plant for a decade before approving it.

items.explanation: The evidence is *reported* cases, and the conclusion is about illness, so the argument is only as good as the assumption that reporting held steady while illness fell. B secures exactly that, in both towns and across the whole period, which is why it is the strongest. A is the trap: it explains how the plant could work, but a plausible mechanism adds little when a rival explanation for the *numbers* is still open. C cuts the other way — more people should mean more cases, though it does not settle the reporting question. D removes one small difference between the towns without touching the reporting gap, and E is history with no bearing on the inference.

items.stem:
City planner: Building a light-rail line will reduce traffic congestion downtown, because every comparable city that built one saw congestion fall within five years.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the five years after their light-rail lines opened, the comparable cities adopted no other measures aimed at reducing downtown traffic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Light-rail construction in the comparable cities was completed ahead of schedule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A majority of downtown business owners in the planner's city favor the light-rail proposal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the comparable cities, congestion fell more sharply in outlying neighborhoods than downtown.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposed line will cost less per mile than any of the comparable cities' lines.

items.explanation: The argument infers that light rail caused the congestion drop from the fact that the two went together in comparable cities. A strengthens it by ruling out the most natural alternative explanation: if nothing else was done about traffic, the rail line is the likeliest cause. B (schedule), C (popularity) and E (cost) do not bear on whether rail reduces congestion. D, if anything, weakens: the effect showed up where the line was not.
items.contrast_note: Same argument as the Weaken version. There, the key supplied an alternative cause for the congestion drop (a second policy enacted at the same time). Here the task is reversed, so the key does the reverse job: it rules alternative causes out. Notice that the cost and popularity choices are wrong in both directions, because neither touches the causal link the argument rests on.

items.stem:
City planner: Building a light-rail line will reduce traffic congestion downtown, because every comparable city that built one saw congestion fall within five years.

The planner's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Light rail is the most cost-effective way for a city to reduce downtown congestion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fall in congestion in the comparable cities was not entirely due to factors unrelated to their light-rail lines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every city that builds a light-rail line sees downtown congestion fall within five years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Downtown congestion in the planner's city has been increasing for at least five years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residents of the comparable cities preferred light rail to expanded bus service.

items.explanation: The argument moves from 'congestion fell after rail was built' to 'rail will reduce congestion', which needs the drop to have had something to do with the rail. Negate B — the drop was entirely due to unrelated factors — and the argument collapses, so B is required. A and C are stronger than the argument needs (it never claims rail is best, or that the effect is universal). D and E are outside the argument's scope.
items.contrast_note: Same argument as the Weaken and Strengthen versions, now asked for what it silently relies on. The Weaken key attacked the causal link with a rival cause; the necessary assumption is the modest denial of exactly that attack — rival causes did not do all the work. The two 'too strong' choices here would be fine Strengthen answers, which is the trap: a claim that would help an argument is not thereby one it needs.

items.stem:
Lawyer: To win the appeal, the defendant must show either that the trial court misapplied the statute or that the jury was improperly instructed. The trial court did not misapply the statute. So if the defendant wins the appeal, then the jury was improperly instructed.

The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A defendant can show that a trial court misapplied a statute only if the court in fact did so.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a trial court misapplies a statute, the defendant will be able to show that it did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The defendant will win the appeal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The jury was improperly instructed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An appeal cannot be won on the ground of improper jury instruction alone.

items.explanation: The premises say winning requires showing one of two things, and that the court did not misapply the statute. The gap is between the court not misapplying the statute and the defendant being unable to show that it did. A closes it: no misapplication means no showing of one, so the only route left is the jury instruction. B bridges the wrong direction. C and D merely assert parts of the conclusion. E contradicts the premises.
items.contrast_note: Same argument as the Necessary Assumption version. That task asked for the modest claim the argument cannot do without (that the two listed grounds are the only grounds). This task asks for a claim strong enough to guarantee the conclusion, so the key is a conditional that bridges the actual gap between 'the court did not misapply the statute' and 'the defendant cannot show that it did'. The reversed conditional is the planted trap: it links the same two terms in the direction that proves nothing.
